summary: A single author from Happiest Minds Technologies proposes Rel(AI)Build, a Node.js 'deterministic control plane' that sits above coding harnesses. It has five parts: a SHA-256 content-addressed registry of agent definitions with an HMAC lockfile and an audit log; five permission tiers checked at compile time; regex command and path blocklists wired into Claude Code PreToolUse and Cursor beforeShellExecution hooks; a phase state machine (spec, design, implementation, test, review, security, finalize) with four human gates, delegation receipts, a 3-iteration auto-fix cap and a requirement-to-file-to-test trace; and a compiler from one canonical definition to seven IDE formats. The evidence is conformance tests on 10, 15 and 20 self-constructed violations, a prevalence study of config files in 10,008 public GitHub repos, and a single drift vignette. There is no developer-outcome or comparative evaluation.

claims.claim: Agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components: 10.1% of tracked paths are fork-adjusted SHA-256 exact duplicates across repositories, and 75.5% of clone pairs cross organisational boundaries
claims.evidence: Table 10. The denominator is all tracked config paths (n≈30,581 = 6,145 agent configs + 24,436 GitHub Actions workflows), so about 80% of it is CI workflow files. No duplicate rate for agent configs alone is reported. The 75.5% cross-org share is computed on raw, non-fork-filtered pairs and has no base rate. The corpus has 10,008 repos across 9,357 orgs (about 1.07 repos per org), so nearly any random pair of repos is cross-org by construction, and 75.5% may actually indicate within-org enrichment.

claims.claim: Agent configs are rarely revised: 58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month against CI workflows after age normalisation
claims.evidence: Tables 10-11 and the cohort-matched subset (0.4 vs 0.75) partly bound the age confound. However, the 95% CIs treat 6,145 files as independent when they sit in only 846 repos (5,441 are .claude/** files), so the intervals are too narrow.

claims.claim: Fewer than 1% of agent configs declare permission boundaries, vs 33% of Actions workflows
claims.evidence: 31 true positives after removing 6 of 37 parser hits. Actions has a native permissions key, while most agent-config files are prose markdown with no permission syntax. The file-level denominator is dominated by .claude/** markdown, so the comparison is between unlike artifacts. The authors label it indicative.

claims.claim: Each mechanism enforces its stated invariant (tamper gate, tier checks, blocklist, phase-order and delegation gates)
claims.evidence: §6.2: 10/10 tamper cases, 15/15 over-privileged declarations and 20/20 synthetic blocklist strings were caught. The author concedes these are hand-written detectors matched against inputs built to be detected, with no field or adversarial evaluation.

claims.claim: Phase-gate checks are hard-coded and 'cannot be bypassed via persuasive LLM prompting'
claims.evidence: No adversarial test. The gates only see what the agent reports through workflow-state and trace-update CLI/MCP calls. phase-state.json is a workspace file that an agent with write access could edit. §4.5 itself admits that trace linkage is an honour-system component.

The §4.1 verifier recomputes a truncated SHA-256 of each line's own content. Nothing links a line to its predecessor, so deleting, reordering or rewriting-and-rehashing lines goes undetected. As described, the mechanism is per-line checksums, not a hash chain.

claims.claim: Governance of the configuration layer must be deterministic and tool-agnostic, not delegated to further LLM orchestration
claims.evidence: Argued from first principles ('a non-deterministic component cannot serve as a trustworthy control'). No comparison with an LLM-governed or ungoverned arm is reported. A Cursor-only comparator arm was run (Appendix D), but its outcomes are withheld to ancillary files.

patterns.note: Fixed phase state machine over phases {0,1,3,4,5,7,8}. Guards: ordering, end-without-start, delegation receipts, spec-reviewer gate, post-delegation security scan, a 3-iteration fix cap, and four human pauses. The only evidence is conformance tests showing that out-of-order or receipt-less transitions raise errors, plus a single build (N=1) where the Phase-8 gate caught one acceptance criterion with no test trace. No comparison against a plain agent loop: the Cursor-only comparator arm was run, but its results are not reported in the paper. Phase-gate overhead is unmeasured (§9.2).

Five permission tiers enforced at compile time, and attack-derived regex blocklists deployed as Claude Code PreToolUse and Cursor beforeShellExecution hooks (failClosed). Codex, Windsurf, OpenCode and Kiro do not enforce the emitted permissions at runtime (§4.6). Evidence is conformance-only.
Four human-in-the-loop gates (after spec, design, pre-release and merge), with rejection and rollback semantics. Benefit and overhead are not measured.
spec.md is content-hashed at approval, and spec-drift checks compare the git diff against files registered to acceptance criteria. Shown only in the N=1 vignette.
trace.json maps each acceptance criterion to its files and tests. The linkage depends on the agent cooperatively calling trace-update. Unregistered edits are detected after the fact, not prevented.
JSONL audit log of CLI mutations. It is described as hash-chained, but the verifier only checks per-line self-hashes.
Blocklists target workspace-trust and git-hook injection (git config, core.hooksPath). The paper states that prompt injection is not solved and puts residual risk at Medium. No attack evaluation.
Hard 3-iteration auto-fix cap (configurable 1-5). It is justified by an 'Anonymous, 2025' debugging-decay citation, not by the author's own measurement.
The prevalence study describes CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules and copilot-instructions files as rarely revised and often copied. It is descriptive and says nothing about effectiveness.
Governance operations are exposed through both a CLI (authoritative) and an MCP server (in-IDE).

methodology.sample: Conformance: 237 canonical agent definitions x 7 targets; 10 tamper, 15 over-privilege and 20 blocklist injected cases. Prevalence: 10,008 public repos (846 with any agent config), 6,145 agent-config files and 24,436 Actions workflow files. Vignette: one 26-AC FastAPI build.
methodology.baselines: None for the system. The prevalence study compares agent configs with GitHub Actions workflows in the same repos. A Cursor-only comparator arm was run in Appendix D, but its results are withheld from the paper.
methodology.models: No model is evaluated. The vignette states that 'GitHub Copilot is the AI model within Cursor', which leaves the actual model unspecified.
methodology.variance: Binomial 95% CIs on prevalence proportions, computed as if files were independent despite clustering in 846 repos. None for conformance or the vignette.
methodology.languages: Implementation in Node.js; definitions cover 14 stacks including Java/Spring Boot; vignette in Python/FastAPI

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint, single author, not peer reviewed
standards.artifacts: Prevalence dataset, report.json, analysis pipeline and figure scripts on Zenodo and arXiv ancillary files. The Rel(AI)Build implementation source is not linked. The comparator walkthrough exists only as an ancillary PDF.

biases.detail: The headline duplicate rate is computed over all tracked paths, about 80% of which are Actions workflows, yet it is reported as an agent-config finding. The cross-org share has no base rate, even though about 1.07 repos per org makes nearly all pairs cross-org. The permission comparison sets a native Actions key against prose markdown.
Conformance cases were built by the author to be caught by the author's own detectors (acknowledged in §6.2).
A Cursor vs Cursor+Rel(AI)Build comparison was run, but its outcomes are excluded from the paper and appear only in an ancillary report.
'Hash-chained' describes per-line self-hashes, and 'cannot be bypassed via prompting' is asserted for gates that only see agent-reported state.
File-level CIs ignore clustering of 6,145 files within 846 repositories.
The only end-to-end use of the lifecycle is one N=1 build.
The time and token overhead of phase gates and human pauses is not measured (§9.2).
The system under study (Rel(AI)Build CLI/MCP) is not released; only the prevalence pipeline is.

coi.affiliations: Happiest Minds Technologies (IT services), AIP Centre of Excellence; single author
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Rel(AI)Build, the author's company framework, which has a company compliance companion document (Madatha 2026b). Cursor, Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, Windsurf, OpenCode and Kiro are described, not evaluated.
coi.detail: The author presents his employer's own system with no independent replication. This is mitigated by explicitly scoping claims to conformance and disclaiming outcome superiority, but the comparison data that could test that claim is withheld.

verdict_reason: Useful as a concrete design reference: deterministic phase gates, receipts, hooks across hosts, and one-definition-to-many-host compilation, with candid trust-boundary notes. As evidence it is weak. The prevalence headline is mis-denominated and lacks a base rate, the 'hash-chained' and 'cannot be bypassed' claims go beyond the mechanism described, and the only outcome comparison was run but withheld.
applicability: On the DAG question, this is a P36 process-level state machine that gates feature work (spec, design, implementation, test, review, security, finalize). It is not an execution DAG for the coding task, and the paper gives no evidence that it beats a plain agent loop on quality, defects or time. The transferable parts for the Java multi-repo team are: (1) let a deterministic CLI own phase state and refuse transitions that lack receipts (spec review, test trace, security scan), which matches qr's 'LLM proposes, CLI verifies'; (2) compile one canonical agent definition to Cursor, Claude Code and Codex formats for mixed hosts; (3) keep a per-acceptance-criterion file and test trace for SDD. The team should also avoid two weaknesses in the design. Gates should verify independently, using git diff and CI results rather than agent-reported state files. And Codex and several other hosts will not enforce the emitted permissions. Nothing here addresses coordination across 4+ repositories, since lockfiles and state are per-project.

conflicts_with.detail: Position tension: SPOQ governs work through an LLM-generated YAML task DAG with LLM-scored planning and code validation, whereas Rel(AI)Build argues governance must not be delegated to LLM orchestration. Neither paper runs the comparison.
Agrees in direction: 'Init Fossilization' smell vs 58% single-commit agent configs. Neither shows staleness harms agent outcomes.
Agrees in direction: context rot in config files, consistent with low revision rates here.
